questions.question: For left-continuity at $x_0$, which side of $x_0$ is used?
options: Only points $x$ with $x_0-\delta \lt x \le x_0$.
Only points $x$ with $x_0 \le x \lt x_0+\delta$.
Only points $x$ with $x = x_0+\delta$.
Only points outside every interval around $x_0$.

questions.question: At an integer $k$, which one-sided continuity statement is true for the floor function $f(x) = \lfloor x\rfloor$?
options: $f$ is left-continuous at $k$.
$f$ is right-continuous at $k$.
$f$ is left-continuous but not right-continuous at $k$.
$f$ has no one-sided continuity at $k$.

questions.question: How is full continuity at an interior point related to one-sided continuity?
options: Full continuity holds whenever the left and right limits exist and agree.
Full continuity requires either left- or right-continuity.
Full continuity implies neither left- nor right-continuity.
Full continuity requires both left-continuity and right-continuity.

questions.question: Which value is used as the target in one-sided continuity at $x_0$?
options: An arbitrary number unrelated to $f(x_0)$.

questions.question: Let $f(0) = 3$ and $f(x) = 3+x$ for $x \gt 0$. Is $f$ right-continuous at $0$?
options: No, because $f(x)$ is not constant for $x \gt 0$.
Yes, because $f(x)$ approaches $3 = f(0)$ as $x\downarrow0$.
No, because $f$ is not defined for $x \lt 0$.
Yes, because every function is right-continuous at $0$.

questions.question: Why does right-continuity at $x_0$ require $f$ to be defined on some interval $[x_0,x_0+r)$?
options: Because right-continuity is only defined for polynomial functions, which are defined on whole intervals around $x_0$.
Because the definition needs values of $f(x)$ for points approaching $x_0$ from the right, including $x_0$.
Because the value of $f(x_0)$ must be excluded.
Because right-continuity requires values on the left of $x_0$.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the link between one-sided limits and one-sided continuity?
options: Right-continuity means the left-hand limit exists and equals $x_0$.
Right-continuity means the right-hand limit exists and equals $f(x_0)$.
One-sided continuity does not involve limits.
One-sided continuity only concerns whether $f(x_0)$ is defined.

questions.question: Let $f(0) = 1$, $f(x) = 1$ for $x \gt 0$, and $f(x) = 0$ for $x \lt 0$. Which statement is true at $0$?
options: $f$ is left-continuous but not right-continuous at $0$.
$f$ is right-continuous but not left-continuous at $0$.
$f$ is continuous from both sides at $0$.
$f$ is not right-continuous because $f(0)$ is defined.

questions.question: At an integer $k$, the ceiling function $g(x) = \lceil x\rceil$ has which one-sided continuity property?
options: $g$ is left-continuous at $k$ but not right-continuous at $k$.
$g$ is right-continuous at $k$ but not left-continuous at $k$.
$g$ is neither left-continuous nor right-continuous at $k$.
$g$ is right-continuous at $k$ because $g(k+1) = g(k)$.

options: $x_0-\delta \lt x\le x_0$
$x_0\le x \lt x_0+\delta$
$x \lt x_0-\delta$

options: $x_0\le x \lt x_0+\delta$
$x \gt x_0+\delta$
$x_0-\delta \lt x\le x_0$

questions.question: Why is one-sided continuity useful at boundary points?
options: Boundary points always have two-sided neighbourhoods in the domain
Only one side of the domain may be available near the boundary
Continuity cannot be discussed at boundary points
Function values at boundary points are never used

Continuity from one side means the one-sided behaviour matches the actual value at $x_0$
The target must be $0$ for every function
